Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more. Aug 16, 2026 — 5:30 AM ET Every year, consumers are pressured into upgrading from last year’s phone to this year’s. With the launch of the Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro owners are now feeling this squeeze. I’ll admit, Google’s alluring marketing and promise of progress are tempting. Wanting the latest and greatest product isn’t intrinsically a negative desire. But Android makers are struggling to deliver a steady stream of annual advancements, and this crunch is starting to show. There’s almost no more blood to be squeezed from this stone. That’s how I see the Google Pixel 11 Pro. While it is certainly new, it lands with a few more lines in its specs and feature sheets, and packs some catchy aesthetic additions, there isn’t much more to be had if you already own a Pixel 10 Pro. If you’re still rocking a Pixel 10 Pro, fret not. There’s plenty of life left in Google’s 2025 flagship. Here’s why you should hold onto it for now. The tech world continues to grapple with the RAM shortage pickle. There’s not enough to go around, and the existing stock is costing manufacturers an arm and a leg. Unfortunately, the Pixel 11 Pro’s base model is a victim of this, and consumers will feel the pain. While the cheapest Pixel 11 Pro now offers consumers 256GB of internal storage — double that provided by the lowest Pixel 10 Pro model — it packs 4GB less RAM. Granted, 12GB of RAM is still plenty for most users’ modest needs, but given that the Pixel 10 Pro packs 16GB across the board, comparatively, multitasking and RAM-hungry AI features will take a hit. The downgrade is perhaps understandable given the global crunch, but I can’t support this year’s price increase, which has also arrived uninvited. The Pixel 11 Pro is $100 more than the Pixel 10 Pro. I don’t know about you, but 4GB less RAM and 128GB more storage doesn’t warrant that premium. The wonderful thing about modern smartphones is the sheer length of the after-sales support consumers receive, specifically that software update window. Google phones have received seven years of Android upgrades and updates since 2023, and this broad span includes the Pixel 10 Pro. Given it was launched in 2025, the Pixel 10 Pro will remain under the ambit of Google’s software support net until at least 2031 — that’s plenty of time to consider picking up the Pixel 11 Pro in the future, or even the Pixel 16 Pro if you see out the entirety of that window. It’s also worth noting that many of the forthcoming software features debuting on the Pixel 11 Pro could still make it to the Pixel 10 Pro. We’re seeing Google hold back certain keystone features from previous models to encourage users to upgrade, but if you’re not enchanted by AI smarts, is it really such a bad thing if the Pixel 10 Pro doesn’t get the Pixel 11 Pro’s toys? One of the Pixel 11 Pro and XL’s marquee features this year is a notification light. Yes, folks, it’s the early 2000s all over again. Initially referred to as Pixel Glow and officially called HiLight, it’s an LED circle that sits on the phone’s camera visor and lights up in various colors when you receive a notification or when Gemini is active. At launch, the feature has an incredibly brief list of use cases, but Google notes that more capabilities are in the works. The biggest issue with HiLight is that it knocks another fan-favorite feature off Pixel phones. The Pixel 11 Pro does not feature a thermometer. While this feature was itself maligned by many when it launched, it provides useful functionality to swathes of users. Google argues that with each new launch, it works to ensure the Pixel offering is as “helpful to as many people as possible.” If you think the thermometer has more utility than a notification LED at the rear of the phone, stick with the Pixel 10 Pro. There’s some great news for Pixel camera aficionados this year. The Pixel 11 Pro receives a “new image sensor“ for the 50MP main camera, and a new, larger image sensor with “30% improved light sensitivity,” 5x Portrait Mode, and 120x Pro Zoom for the 48MP telephoto snapper. This, along with a host of smarts thanks to the Tensor G6 and cloud processing, makes the Pixel 11 Pro a compelling imaging tool. Despite its marketing hype, it remains far too early to tell whether these theoretical upgrades yield markedly better practical performance across all snapping scenarios. The Pixel 10 Pro remains a stellar snapper, and no new phone will affect its results. Even if you don’t upgrade, you’ll be able to capture incredible scenes with the primary 50MP snapper and the 48MP telephoto. It’s also worth noting that the ultrawide doesn’t see any upgrade between the two phones. We’ll certainly pit the Pixel 11 Pro against the Pixel 10 Pro in a head-to-head camera comparison, but I’d certainly practice calm if you’re stirred by Google’s early imaging marketing claims. Alongside the Pixel 11 series, Google has launched the new Pixel Watch 5 and its first first-party location tracker in the Pixel Tag. Importantly, if you wish to use any of these products with your Pixel phone, you needn’t have a Pixel 11 phone in your pocket — they’re compatible with the Pixel 10 Pro and phones older than it, too. The Pixel Tag, when used via the Find Hub network, is compatible with devices running Android 9.0 or newer and Bluetooth 6.0 or newer. This certainly includes Google’s 2025 smartphone. The Pixel Tag goes on sale in November for $99. Remember that $100 premium I mentioned placed on the Pixel 11 Pro this year? I certainly think it’s better spent on a pack of Google’s new location tags. Finally, I urge you to practice the one thing we, as tech enthusiasts, don’t do nearly as much as we should: waiting. The Pixel 11 Pro is the latest Pixel — that’s undeniable, but it likely won’t be the last Pixel. It’ll hold this position for at most 12 months, until the Pixel 12 Pro arrives. Waiting gives you the advantage of viewing and understanding any hardware and software bugs that arise on the new device after launch, the prevailing feelings of those who have purchased one, and, more importantly, allows the phone to depreciate ever so slightly. In a few months, you’ll be able to take advantage of any sales Google may offer and use Pixel 11 Pros dumped by those constantly clamoring for the newest Android handset. In short, you’ll be able to grab a Pixel 11 Pro below the list price if you wait to purchase one. Of course, you can only really take your time if you don’t explicitly need a phone right now, but if you own a Pixel 10 Pro — a phone that, as I’ve demonstrated, still has plenty of life in it — it certainly won’t hurt. The Pixel 11 Pro is here, but I do believe you should enjoy your Pixel 10 Pro while you have it. Do you agree? The Washington Commanders opened the preseason on Friday with a 20-7 win over the Miami Dolphins. After Miami scored on its first possession, the Dolphins would go the next 11 possessions without a score. During that time, the Commanders intercepted three passes and forced a turnover on downs. It was the type of defensive performance — preseason or not — Washington fans haven’t seen in recent years. Most of the Commanders’ starters did not play. With the two teams having a joint practice only two days earlier, head coach Dan Quinn chose to give his backups and roster hopefuls a chance. Some of those backups and roster hopefuls took advantage of the opportunity, while others still have some work to do. Which player helped his cause on Friday? Which ones still have work to do? Here’s our preseason Week 1 stock report. Undrafted rookie running back Robert Henry Jr. (12-75-1 YD) and sixth-round pick Kaytron Allen (23-85-1 TD) combined for 158 rushing yards and two touchdowns. If we go by past years, the Commanders will likely keep four running backs. Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White are roster locks. Jeremy McNichols isn’t a lock, but Washington loves him. He delivers in every aspect when his number is called. So, Allen and Henry could be battling for one spot, with the other potentially heading to the practice squad. It was a great night for the rookie backs, especially Henry. Sam Hartman had a tremendous college career between Wake Forest and Notre Dame. But he doesn’t physically have the arm strength to play at the NFL level. Washington has kept him on the practice squad for the last two seasons. Hartman had a rough start on Friday but played better as the game progressed. Unfortunately for him, it won’t be enough, as rookie Athan Kaliakmanis looked like he belonged. Hartman is going to need to show much more to even remain on the practice squad. The rookie sixth-round pick came off the bench and looked good. Yes, it was against Miami’s backups, but Gulbin did his job and made some key blocks in both the running and passing games. Go back and watch that Henry touchdown from above. Look for No. 66. Considering Washington’s concerns at center, Gulbin should start next week’s game and get some runs against Detroit’s starters, even if it is for only one series. That’s how you evaluate his progress. There’s a reason that Good-Jones has been around the NFL for several seasons and has barely played. That’s not a knock on him. He’s good enough to make a roster and serve as a reserve interior lineman, but there is no way Washington could trust going into the season with him as the backup center. Good-Jones’s play strength is an issue. Quan Martin needed a good night. The talent is there. After what looked like a potential breakout year in 2024, big things were expected last season. He regressed badly. So did almost everyone else on last year’s defense. He hasn’t exactly stood out in training camp, but sometimes that can be deceiving. Martin made more plays than just the interception in Friday’s game. He’s back in the mix, alongside Jeremy Reaves, to start at free safety. Based on Friday’s game, I’d rank him ahead of Will Harris. It’s fair to ask if Newton will ever live up to being the former No. 36 overall pick. It’s also fair to wonder if the foot injuries Newton suffered have impacted his long-term potential. He flashed in the Dallas game last season. Outside of that, he’s mostly been a guy. I don’t see the Commanders cutting Newton. He could be a trade candidate. He will be given every chance to shine, even if it keeps him on the field longer in preseason games. A second-year former UDFA, Barber was on the practice squad for much of last season. Ironically, in the same game where Newton excelled, Barber also stood out. Entering camp, Barber was more of a practice squad candidate. He was outstanding against the Dolphins. Very active against the run and in the pass rush. Barber has a real shot to make the 53. Turn out the lights, the party’s over. Undrafted rookie Drew Stevens has already won Washington’s kicker job. Both kickers were perfect against Miami, but even Moody’s make wasn’t easy. He doinked it in from only 29 yards out. Stevens easily made his only FG attempt from 41 yards right down the middle. Moody will remain on the roster until the end, but there’s no way the Commanders are letting Stevens go in favor of Moody. Certain players just always catch your eye. That’s 10-year veteran Antonio Hamilton Sr. After signing with the Commanders last season, injuries forced Hamilton onto the field. He was terrific on special teams and, truthfully, one of Washington’s better corners last season. NFL teams may not want to keep 33-year-old cornerbacks over younger players, but everything you saw from Hamilton on Friday exemplifies what head coach Dan Quinn says about what he looks for in players. With two more performances like Friday’s, Hamilton will make it hard on GM Adam Peters.
